--- execute: warning: false knitr: opts_knit: global.par: true opts_chunk: comment: '' fig.width: 5.5 fig.height: 5.5 out.width: 80% --- # Introduction to **ggplot2** {#sec-ggplot2} **`ggplot2`**, created by Hadley Wickham [@wickham2011ggplot2], follows the [Grammar of Graphics](https://www.springer.com/statistics/computational/book/978-0-387-24544-7) approach of Leland Wilkinson [@wilkinson2012grammar]. It therefore features a very different syntax from base R graphics functions seen in @sec-basegraphics. It is based on the `grid` graphics package, which, perhaps confusingly, is included in base R.

The general idea is to start by defining the data and then add and/or modify graphical elements in a stepwise manner, which allows one to build complex and layered visualizations. A simplified interface to `ggplot` graphics is provided in the `qplot()` function of **`ggplot2`**. This chapter focuses on the basics of the `ggplot()` function, which is more flexible and powerful. ::: callout-warning Do not try to combine base R graphics and **`ggplot2`** graphics in the same plot. They are based on different graphics engines and are not compatible. ::: ## Setup ### Packages Load **`ggplot2`** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(ggplot2) library(dplyr) library(tidyr) library(tibble) # You can alternatively load all tidyverse packages with: # library(tidyverse) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ### Synthetic Data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(data.table) set.seed(2022) dt <- data.table( PID = sample(8001:9000, size = 100), Age = rnorm(100, mean = 33, sd = 8), Weight = rnorm(100, mean = 70, sd = 9), SysBP = rnorm(100, mean = 110, sd = 6), DiaBP = rnorm(100, mean = 80, sd = 6), Sex = factor(sample(c("Female", "Male"), size = 100, replace = TRUE)) ) dt[, SysBP := SysBP + 0.5 * Age] dt[Sex == "Male", Weight := Weight + rnorm(.N, mean = 16, sd = 1.5)] dt[Sex == "Male", Age := Age + rnorm(.N, mean = 6, sd = 1.8)] dt <- as_tibble(dt) ``` ::: Define a color palette, `palette_`, and a version of the same palette at 2/3 transparency, `palette_a`, for use in plots: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} palette_ <- c("#43A4AC", "#FA9860") palette_a <- adjustcolor(palette_, 0.666) ``` ::: ::: callout-note Confusingly, `ggplot2` uses the `aes()` function, short for aesthetics, to define the plot data. ::: ## Grammar of Graphics The general syntax of a `ggplot` command is as follows: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_*() + theme_*() + scale_*() ``` ::: Where: - `data` is the data frame or tibble containing the data to be plotted. - `aes(x, y)` defines which variables are mapped to which axes, etc. as well as other mappings, like color, shape, size, etc. - `geom_*()` specifies the type of geometric object to be used for the plot, such as points, lines, bars, etc. - `theme_*()` allows customization of the plot's appearance, such as background, grid lines, text size, etc. - `scale_*()` allows customization of the scales used for the axes and other aesthetics, such as color scales, axis limits, etc. ## Box plot `ggplot` requires a categorical x-axis to draw boxplots. This means we need to convert our dataset from wide to long format. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} dt_long <- dt |> pivot_longer( cols = c("SysBP", "DiaBP"), names_to = "Measure", values_to = "Value" ) dt_long ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 200 × 6 PID Age Weight Sex Measure Value 1 8228 28.5 82.2 Male SysBP 122. 2 8228 28.5 82.2 Male DiaBP 79.1 3 8435 50.1 72.6 Female SysBP 136. 4 8435 50.1 72.6 Female DiaBP 84.3 5 8718 31.0 73.0 Female SysBP 124. 6 8718 31.0 73.0 Female DiaBP 78.1 7 8823 30.0 77.5 Male SysBP 126. 8 8823 30.0 77.5 Male DiaBP 80.9 9 8843 40.5 86.7 Male SysBP 133. 10 8843 40.5 86.7 Male DiaBP 68.6 # ℹ 190 more rows ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt_long, aes(Measure, Value)) + geom_boxplot() p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: We can specify `color` and `fill` to change the color of the boxplot border and fill, respectively. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt_long, aes(Measure, Value)) + geom_boxplot(color = palette_[1:2], fill = palette_a[1:2]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ### Grouped boxplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(x = Sex, y = Age)) + geom_boxplot(colour = palette_[2:1], fill = palette_a[2:1]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ## Histogram ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(Age)) + geom_histogram() p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: We can specify the number of bins to use with the `bins` argument and the border and fill colors with `color` and `fill`, respectively, as above. `xlab()` can be used to define the x-axis label. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(Age)) + geom_histogram(bins = 24, color = palette_[1], fill = palette_a[1]) + xlab("Age (years)") p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ### Grouped Histogram ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(x = Age, fill = Sex)) + geom_histogram(bins = 24, position = "identity") p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: `scale_fill_manual` can be used to define the colors of the bars: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(x = Age, fill = Sex)) + geom_histogram(bins = 24, position = "identity") + scale_fill_manual(values = palette_a[2:1]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: `position = "identity"` displays overlapping bars. Alternatively, `position = "dodge"` can be used to display groups' bars side by side instead. Finally, `position = "stack"`, is the (unfortunate) default and results in vertically stacked bars, which can be useful for showing totals but otherwise confusing. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(x = Age, fill = Sex)) + geom_histogram(bins = 24, position = "dodge") + scale_fill_manual(values = palette_a[2:1]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(x = Age, fill = Sex)) + geom_histogram(bins = 24, position = "stack") + scale_fill_manual(values = palette_a[2:1]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ## Density plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(x = Age)) + geom_density(color = palette_[1], fill = palette_a[1]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ### Grouped density plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(x = Age, fill = Sex)) + geom_density(color = NA) + scale_fill_manual(values = palette_a[2:1]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ## Barplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} schools <- data.frame(UCSF = 4, Stanford = 7, Penn = 12) ``` ::: `ggplot2` requires an explicit column in the data that define the categorical x-axis: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} schools_df <- data.frame( University = factor(colnames(schools), levels = c("UCSF", "Stanford", "Penn")), N_schools = as.numeric(schools[1, ]) ) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(schools_df, aes(University, N_schools)) + geom_bar( stat = "identity", color = palette_a[1], fill = palette_a[1] ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-20-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ## Scatterplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(Age, SysBP)) + geom_point(color = palette_a[1]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-21-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ### Grouped Scatterplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(Age, SysBP, col = Sex)) + geom_point() + scale_color_manual(values = palette_[2:1]) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ## Themes `ggplot2` includes several built-in themes that can be applied to plots to change their overall appearance. The default theme is `theme_grey()`, but other popular themes include `theme_minimal()`, `theme_bw()`, and `theme_classic()`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(Age, SysBP)) + geom_point() + theme_minimal() # or theme_bw(), theme_classic(), etc. ``` ::: ## Faceting Faceting allows you to create multiple plots based on the values of one or more categorical variables. This is useful for comparing distributions or relationships across different groups. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(Age, SysBP)) + geom_point() + facet_wrap(~Sex) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-24-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ## Adding labels ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(Age, SysBP)) + geom_point() + labs( title = "Systolic BP vs Age", x = "Age (years)", y = "Systolic BP (mmHg)" ) p ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](ggplot2_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=80%} ::: ::: ## Save plot to file We'll use the grouped boxplot example from above to show how to save each type of plot to file, using a PDF output as an example. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p <- ggplot(dt, aes(x = Sex, y = Age)) + geom_boxplot(colour = palette_[2:1], fill = palette_a[2:1]) ggsave("Age_by_Sex_ggplot.pdf", p, width = 5.5, height = 5.5, scale = 1, units = "in") ``` ::: ## See also - Base R Graphics ([@sec-basegraphics]) - Introduction to **plotly** ([@sec-plotly]) ## Resources - [ggplot2 Documentation](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/)
